transcript:
Header: 2026-07-29 15:00 UTC | Duration: 52m | Attendees: Jordan, Priya (Redwood); Carlos, Leah, Tom (BlueWave)

Summary (auto): agreed short-term mitigations for TTFT spikes; plan for int8 kernel canary and prefix cache test.

00:00 Jordan: okay, welcome everyone, thanks for making time. Today we want to go over the TTFT anomalies from last week's run and the streaming hiccups you hit during the midday burst. Priya will walk through traces and proposed mitigations.
00:18 Priya: yeah hi all, I pulled the traces. quick note, some of the labeling in the trace exporter got swapped so you'll see "Speaker 3" on a few spans, ignore that.
00:27 Carlos: yeah we saw several slow first tokens between 120 and 380 ms—most were around 180 but the 95th and 99th look bad.
00:35 Priya: exactly. baseline for the 8k model on dedicated nodes is around 90 to 120 ms median, but when microbursts hit the batcher window expands and we see these 95/99 spikes.
00:48 Tom: and those correspond to the streaming handshake timeouts? like the initial websocket handshake pause?
00:53 Priya: in some cases yes, in others it's the kernel selection path. we instrumented the runtime: request comes in -> routing -> batching -> kernel pick -> kv cache lookup -> first-token emission. the latency lumps up when batching waits for additional requests or when the runtime selects a fallback kernel (int8) and warms the plan.
01:15 Leah: warming the plan — is that the compilation jitter we saw last month? should be precompiled on the fleet.
01:22 Priya: normally yes, but if the model variant hasn't been used on that node for a while the JIT path still has a small compile or kernel init cost. also there's an observed blob where KV cache misses cascade.
01:35 Carlos: hmm. so is it more of a batching policy or cache miss problem?
01:40 Priya: both. our hypothesis is: sequence length distribution during the midday jobs shifted higher which increased per-request token budget and the batcher held open windows to try to amortize tokens. that increases TTFT for some fast-path requests.
01:58 Jordan: can you break down a concrete example? like request profile and what the batcher did?
02:03 Priya: sure. on Tuesday we saw median seq len 18 but 30% of requests in the spike had 64+. Batcher window is adaptive based on target latency SLO; it stretched to 40 ms to capture larger ones. a fast single-token prompt arriving during that window got held, bumping its first byte by 35-40 ms. then if the node had a cold kernel we added another 50-70 ms.
02:29 Tom: that matches our logs — we saw a tail at exactly the same timestamps. also there were a couple of 503 fallbacks when the pool spiked.
02:38 Priya: right, and fallbacks triggered model variant routing which sometimes switched to a quantized 7B variant; switching adds another few tens of ms while the runtime remaps weights.
02:48 Carlos: so from a product SLAs standpoint we need to choose: accept slightly higher median with fewer spikes, or force strict TTFT at cost of throughput. what's realistic?
02:57 Jordan: BlueWave, what are your actual SLOs? can you confirm numbers?
03:02 Carlos: we'd like P99 TTFT < 250 ms for customer-facing chat, and P95 < 150 ms. We can tolerate some throughput loss for peak retail flows but need predictable tails.
03:13 Jordan: okay good to know. target plumbing: P99 < 250ms, P95 <150ms. we'll aim mitigation for that.
03:20 Priya: short-term mitigations we proposed: 1) tighten batching window for low-latency routes, 2) enable prefix/KV caching for common prompts to avoid recompute, 3) keep a hot kernel pool for the most-used variants, 4) routing policy to avoid fallback to remote quantized variant unless absolutely necessary.
03:39 Leah: prefix cache looks promising — we have lots of identical system prompts. what's the overhead?
03:43 Priya: minimal. prefix caching stores token-level kvs for prompt prefixes and reuses across requests — reduces time in KV lookup + decode path by ~20-30 ms in our tests. downside: more memory usage on node, but we can scope to high-qps routes.
03:57 Tom: memory trade-off okay if we limit to a few routes. how about the kernel swap canary? int8 looked cheaper but our initial test added jitter.
04:06 Priya: int8 has lower compute latency once warmed, but conversion and occasional dequant ops add jitter on cold path. plan is to do a canary on 10% of traffic in dedicated pool with warmup and continuous background pre-warm.
04:20 Carlos: would that affect quality noticeably? our evals show slight BLEU-ish drop on edge cases.
04:26 Priya: yes small quality delta for some token distributions; Redwood Optimize can flag regressions on your eval set and auto-roll back if score drops past threshold.
04:33 Jordan: side note: we can configure auto-fallback if quality drops; that's part of the rollout.
04:39 (brief crosstalk)
04:45 Priya: okay I want to show a trace snippet — shared link in chat — see span around 10:13:22, you can see batcher held for 42 ms, then kernel init ~62 ms, then first byte out at 180 ms.
05:00 Carlos: yup I opened it. there's also a repeated pattern where sequence-len heavy requests align with certain client endpoints. client side is batching too.
05:12 Leah: ah that's important — our SDK does client-side multiplexing and sometimes piles up long prompts into single requests which changes distribution.
05:19 Jordan: good catch. we should coordinate on client SDK changes; perhaps add a small jitter or split long prompts.
05:26 Tom: we can add jitter but need to measure effect on throughput.
05:29 Priya: next technical idea: early-response fastpath — if model prefix matches a known route we can stream first tokens from cached KV while batcher continues to collect; that reduces TTFT for those requests. it's more complex but doable in the runtime.
05:45 Carlos: sounds promising but engineering heavy. timeline?
05:49 Priya: prototype in 2 sprints, canary in 1 week if we prioritize. alternatively prefix cache + tighten window is quicker.
05:57 Jordan: what's lower lift and likely biggest win?
05:59 Priya: prefix cache + conservative batching window per-route gives biggest immediate win. early fastpath is medium-term. int8 canary could give cost wins but needs careful warmup.
06:12 Leah: on the routing side, can you share the policy that prevents fallback to quantized variant until node is saturated? we had fallbacks cause extra latency and some errors.
06:22 Priya: yes, we have a routing policy template — I'll attach. key knobs: max-concurrent-per-node, aggressive hedging, and fallback-threshold (e.g., only fallback when latency over 600ms or node CPU >85%).
06:36 Jordan: also note we can route by tenant to dedicated pools and keep retail traffic on dedicated and low-latency routes.
06:43 Carlos: ok lets set two route tiers: customer-chat-lowlatency and bulk-analytics-highthroughput.
06:50 Jordan: agreed. customer-chat-lowlatency will have batching window capped at 20 ms, prefix cache enabled, no int8 fallback unless manual override.
06:59 Priya: I'll draft that YAML.
07:03 Tom: about observability, can we get token-level traces exported to our S3? we want to join with our client-side logs.
07:09 Priya: yes we can export traces, but names might be fuzzy — we'll work on consistent span naming. also we'll provide flamegraphs.
07:18 Carlos: great. one more thing: we saw a couple of 5xx in the 2:30 - 3:00pm window when we hit the microburst; are those overload or infra bugs?
07:27 Priya: initial look suggests queue length exceeded a soft cap and we returned 503s from our front-door. the immediate mitigation is to increase burst capacity for that pool and apply hedging so requests go to a cold fallback earlier before the queue saturates.
07:41 Leah: we prefer hedging over increasing cores because of cost. can you simulate hedging behavior?
07:46 Priya: yes that's part of the microburst repro I'll run. includes switching to hedged mode with 2x inflight and canceling slower tail.
07:56 Jordan: timeline recap — Priya runs repro & provides traces; Leah toggles prefix cache; Jordan sends routing policy & cost delta; Carlos confirms SLA and canary window.
08:07 Carlos: confirmed I'll loop in legal for the canary window.
08:10 Tom: one quick question — do you support per-route token quotas to prevent a single client from creating bursty traffic?
08:16 Priya: yes per-route qps and token-burst limits exist; we can set per-api-key rate buckets.
08:22 Leah: perfect. that should help.
08:25 Jordan: any other blockers?
08:27 Carlos: just need the benchmark sheet and scheduling for the canary.
08:30 Jordan: I'll send both after this call.
08:34 Priya: ok I'll start the repro. I'll also include a trace where we intentionally pre-warm int8 kernel to show warm vs cold delta.
08:42 Carlos: thanks, appreciate the quick follow-ups.
08:45 Jordan: thanks everyone. we'll reconvene next Tuesday same time for status and to review the canary results.
08:52 (meeting end)

Notes: transcript shows occasional label errors and filler words; some technical terms transcribed as separate letters (e.g., T T F T) in places. Shared links posted in chat.
